rationale: A wins because it knows where the story stops and where the proof burden begins. Its best line is the discipline in “Get the proof first — a named bank, or a specific compliance/audit confirmation,” while B steps on a rake with “rebuttal anchored in named institutions” when the update names zero institutions. B has useful instincts, but it keeps turning reporting hypotheses into assertions.
gaps_in_A: “Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents” implies displacement and an incumbent set the update does not prove.

“Notion lets EU and Australian enterprise customers keep their data at home” over-compresses data residency into a promise; the update does not say what data, processing, regions, or defaults are covered.
“Four of the five largest US banks are quietly testing Notion” adds “quietly,” which may be true atmospherically but is not in the supplied facts.
Refusing “Notion ships offline-first editing” is too absolute; offline-first can carry a real enterprise reliability angle if tied to regulated-buyer requirements and properly proven.
gaps_in_B: “rebuttal anchored in named institutions” is flatly wrong. The update says four of the five largest US banks run pilots; it names none.
“secure facilities, regulated firms, or intermittent-connectivity environments” invents use cases the update does not supply. Air-gap speculation is especially premature.
“Confluence and SharePoint on the defensive” names specific threatened incumbents without evidence that Notion is replacing them or competing in those RFPs.
“forced to localize data for Europe and Australia” overstates causality. The update says Notion added data residency options, not that regulators or customers forced the move.
